## Mac users
Almost everything here works the same in the Mac Terminal. The exceptions are small: the Linux commands `free` and `nproc` don't exist on a Mac (use `top`, and `sysctl -n hw.ncpu`), `ps aux --sort=...` and `stat -c` are Linux-only forms, and the shell's startup file is `~/.zshrc` instead of `~/.bashrc`.
:::

```{r}

```


and `cd` (change directory) into this new directory

The file system is a tree. You  (via the linux prompt) are always "in" one directory, called the **working directory**. Let's verify we are in the right directory using `pwd` (print [the] working directory).


# Download data

We will start with `covid.csv`, from the New York Times' public repository of COVID-19 data. The file tracks COVID-19 in the United States during 2020: each row gives one county on one day, with the total cases and deaths reported there up to that day. It has about 885,000 rows and takes about 35 MB. We won't use it until much later in this lecture except trivially.

Our first "real" linux command is `curl` (client URL) which downloads whatever is at the web address (a URL) you supply. 

```bash
curl -L -o covid.csv https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nytimes/covid-19-data/master/us-counties-2020.csv
#^^^  ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ ^^^^^^^^^
#  |  cmd options    cmd argument
# linux command
```

A command has three parts: the **command** itself, **options** (also called flags) that change its behavior, and **arguments** that tell it what to act on.

We gave it two options:

- `-L` follows redirects: if the server says the file has moved, `curl` automatically fetches it from the new location.
- `-o covid.csv` saves the download in a file with that name. Without `-o`, `curl` prints the contents to the screen.

You don't have to memorize options like these. Almost every command comes with a manual page that lists them, which you open with `man`:

```bash
man curl      # the full manual page (type /--output to search, q to quit)
curl --help   # a shorter summary (GNU/Linux tools)
```


Now let's make sure the `curl` actually worked i.e. downloaded the website and named it correctly. For this we'll use our next command `ls` (list [contents of a directory]). We will use a few options

```bash
ls
ls -l           # list with "l"ong details (default sort is by alphabetical order)
ls -l -h        # + list with "h"uman readable file sizes
ls -l -h -a     # + list "a"ll including hidden files
ls -lha         # `ls -lha` is the same as `ls -l -h -a` this is my go-to 
ls -lhaS        # my other go-to as it also sorts by size (directory links are 4KB - interesting)
ls -lht         # newest file first (t = sort by time)
ls -lhtr        # oldest first (r reverses any of these)
```

And type of file is it (the filename can lie)?

```bash
file covid.csv            
```

The . and .. are "hidden" and signify special directory entries known as "hard links" that act as shortcuts for file system navigation. The `.` is the current directory. We will use it soon. The `..` is the parent directory e.g.

```bash
cd .    #does nothing as it's changing directory into the current directory
pwd
cd ..   #visit one directory up
pwd
```

An **absolute path** starts from the root, `/` so the following will fail

```bash
cd /lec01
```

This fails because there is no `lec01` directory in the root:

```bash
ls /
```

The following is the listing of all files and directories from the root. If you're a sysadmin, you'll be using logs in the root folder `var` a lot and installing programs to `bin` and `opt`. But this is not a class in linux sysadmin - we only need to know what's useful for the data world.

A **relative path** starts from where you are i.e. beginning with pwd. So

```bash
cd lec01
```

is short for

```bash
cd /home/kapelner/workspace/HUJI_52002_Fall_2026/scratch/lec01
#  ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
#  this is the current working directory 
```

Text file stats via `wc` (word count)

```bash
wc -l covid.csv                # count the number of lines in the file
wc -lwmc covid.csv             # count the number of lines, words, characters, bytes in the file
```

How long does a command take? Put `time` in front of it:

```bash
time wc -l covid.csv
```

`real` is the wall-clock time. We'll use `time` to compare methods as well as other profiling techniques throughout the semester.

Keyboard habits that save hours:

| Key | What it does |
|-----|--------------|
| Ctrl+L or `clear` | Clear the screen |
| Tab | Completes file and command names e.g. wc co<tab> Press twice to see options. |
| ↑ / ↓ | Scroll through previous commands |
| Ctrl+R | Search your command history (Enter to run, Ctrl+R again to get previous, Ctrl+G to clear) |
| Ctrl+C | Stop the running command |
| Ctrl+U | Clear the line |

```bash
history             # list your recent commands
which python3       # where is this program installed?
echo $HOME          # print a variable: your home directory (what "~" means)
echo $PATH          # the directories searched for programs
echo $PATH | grep "bigdata" #we will see what this means later
```

The PATH variable is pretty important. You will be adding directories to it for convenience at times so you don't need to specify absolute path each time you want to run a new program you installed.


How much space are things taking?

```bash
du -sh .                                            # total size of this directory
du -sh ~/workspace/HUJI_52002_Fall_2026             # or of any directory of interest
du -h -d 1 ~/workspace/HUJI_52002_Fall_2026         # size of each subdirectory in repo root, one level deep
df -h                     # free space on every disk and partition (note tmp goes in RAM - clear it regularly!!)
df -h ~                   # free space on the disk holding your home directory (what you actually care about)
```

# Managing files

```bash
touch notes.txt             # create an empty file (or update its timestamp)
ls -alhS
cp notes.txt notes2.txt     # copy a file
ls -alhS
mkdir tmp_dir               # make a directory (we've seen this before)
ls -alhS
cp -r tmp_dir tmp_dir_copy  # copy a directory (-r = recursive)
ls -alhS
mv notes2.txt tmp_dir/      # move a file to another folder
ls -alhS
ls tmp_dir/ -alhS
mv tmp_dir/notes2.txt .     # move it to the working directory (that `.`!)
ls -alhS
mv notes.txt my_notes.txt   # rename (via moving to a new name)
ls -alhS
rm notes.txt                # delete a file
ls -alhS
rm notes2.txt my_notes.txt  # delete multiple files
rm -r tmp_dir               # delete a directory and everything in it (r is for "recursive" which is needed)
ls -alhS
rm tmp_dir_copy             # fails
rm -r tmp_dir_copy 
ls -alhS
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## There is no trash can in the linux shell
`rm` deletes permanently. There is no undo.
:::

**Wildcards.** Often you want a command to act on many files at once: every `.csv` file, or every file whose name starts with `file_`. Instead of typing each name, you type a **pattern**, a short description of the names you mean, and the shell works out which files match. Pattern languages turn up everywhere in data work. The shell's version, called **wildcards** or **globs**, has just three building blocks: `*`, `?` and `[...]`. Later in this lecture, `grep` will search *inside* files using a richer pattern language called **regular expressions**. The two look alike and are easy to confuse: in a wildcard `*` means "any characters", while in a regular expression it means "repeat the previous thing any number of times". For now, wildcards:

```bash
touch tmp.csv file_1.txt file_2.txt file_10.tex   # touch takes several names
ls *.csv            # * matches any run of characters, including none
ls file_?.txt       # ? matches exactly one character: file_1.txt, not file_10
ls file_[12].txt    # [...] matches one character from the set
ls file_[0-9].*     # ranges work too plus other wildcards (the suffix can be anything)
ls file_[!1]*       # [!...] matches one character NOT in the set
ls *_1*             # wildcards can go anywhere in the name
ls file_{1,10}.*    # {a,b} is not a wildcard: the shell writes out both names
echo file_{1,10}.*  # see what a pattern expands to before using it with rm
```

The shell expands a pattern into the matching names *before* the command runs, so `ls *.csv` is really `ls covid.csv tmp.csv`, and `ls *` alone lists the contents of every subdirectory too. Patterns never match names that start with a dot (hidden files) unless you write the dot yourself.

**Finding files:** `find` walks a directory tree and prints every file that passes the tests you give it. The first argument is where to start; everything after it is a test.

```bash
find . -name "*.csv"        # find CSV files in the working directory and its subdirectories
find ~ -name "*.csv"        # all csv files anywhere under my home directory and its subdirectories
                            # (your list will differ; I have a lot of files in my WSL as I use it for all my projects)
find . -type f              # only files...
find . -type d              # ...or only directories
find ~ -maxdepth 1 -type f  # don't descend into subdirectories
find . -size +10M           # files bigger than 10 MB
find . -size -1k            # files smaller than 1 KB (the ones we touched)
find . -empty               # empty files and directories
find . -mmin -30            # modified in the last 30 minutes
find . -mtime +7            # modified more than 7 days ago
find . -newer covid.csv     # modified after covid.csv was
```

Several tests in a row must all hold. Use `-o` for "or" and `-not` to negate. `find` is like its own mini programming language.

```bash
find . -type f -name "*.csv" -size +1M    # all three must hold
find . -name "*.csv" -o -name "*.tex"     # either suffix
find . -type f -not -name "*.csv"         # everything except csv files
```

Once `find` has the files, it can do something with them. `-exec` runs a command on each result, with `{}` standing for the file name:

```bash
find . -name "*.txt" -delete              # delete every match (no confirmation given)
ls -alhS
rm -i *.tex                               # ask before each deletion
```

Searching from `/` reaches directories you are not allowed to read, which produces error messages.

```bash
find / -name "*.csv*"
```

Every program has two separate output channels:

- stdout (channel 1) carries normal results, such as the file names find prints.
- stderr (channel 2) carries error messages, such as "find: '...': Permission denied."

Both go to your screen by default, so they look the same. They are separate streams, though, and the program chooses which one to write each line to. find writes matches to stdout and complaints to stderr. So we want to filter out the errors

```bash
find / -name "*.csv*" 2>/dev/null   # no more clutter from looking at useless directories
```

In 2>/dev/null, the 2> means "redirect channel 2 somewhere else", and /dev/null is a special file that throws away anything written to it. Everything on channel 2 is discarded, and channel 1 is untouched.


**Redirects.** A **redirect** sends a command's input or output somewhere other than the keyboard and screen, usually a file. The symbols are:

- `>` (send stdout to a file), 
- `>>` (add stdout to the end of a file), 
- `2>` (send the stderr to a file) and 
- `<` (receive input from a file). 

Demos:

```bash
echo "hello"                 # prints hello on the screen
echo "hello" > notes.txt     # redirect into a file so nothing printed to terminal because it went into notes.txt
ls -alh
cat notes.txt                # cat is "concatenate" which is used mostly to not concatenate but print to screen instead
echo "again" >> notes.txt    # >> adds the object of redirection to a new line at the end (i.e. "new line append")
wc -l notes.txt
cat notes.txt
echo "oops" > notes.txt      # > replaces the contents: no warning!
cat notes.txt 
```

Redirects work with any command, and a redirected file is created if it doesn't exist:

```bash
ls > listing.txt             # save a directory listing
cat listing.txt
date > today.txt             # save the current date and time
cat today.txt
cat notes.txt notes.txt > twice.txt   # join files into a new file (the original intent of the cat command)
cat twice.txt
ls /nonexistent
ls /nonexistent > err.txt   #can we redirect this output?
cat err.txt                 #no, because redirect by default is stdout, not stderr, it's short for 1>
ls /nonexistent 2> err.txt   # save the error message instead of showing it
cat err.txt
ls . /nonexistent
ls . /nonexistent > out.txt
cat out.txt
ls . /nonexistent 1> out.txt
cat out.txt
ls . /nonexistent 1> out.txt 2> err.txt      # results and errors in two different files
cat out.txt
cat err.txt
ls . /nonexistent > all.txt 2>&1      # results and errors in one file the &1 says direct to where 1 went
cat all.txt
```

More about `cat`... Without file argument(s) it takes input from the keyboard:

```bash
cat                              # start typing... until CTRL+D
cat > keyboard_input.txt         # take the keyboard input as stdin and redirect it as stdout to afile
ls -alh
cat keyboard_input.txt
```

First we will introduce multiline strings. They begin with an arbitrary string which denote the end of input. This is usually
'EOF' (for "end of file"). Thus EOF terminates the input. The "<<" is a redirection in the opposite direction from before. 
It tells cat to take string input and not from the keyboard.

```bash
cat << 'EOF'
line 1
line 2
line 3
EOF
```

Now the following would make sense, but it ruins the "EOF" delimiter 

```bash
cat << 'EOF' ####don't run this
line 1
line 2
line 3
EOF > stream_input.txt
```

So we can direct the output of cat as the first argument

```bash
cat > stream_input.txt << 'EOF'
line 1
line 2
line 3
EOF
ls -alh
cat stream_input.txt
```
**A first shell script.** A shell script is a text file of commands that the shell runs one after another, so a sequence you would otherwise retype can be saved and rerun. Here is the smallest useful one: a file `my_script.sh` with a single line, `touch file1.txt`, which creates an empty file.

```bash
echo "touch file1.txt" > my_script.sh   # sh is the standard extension for "shell script"
                                        # although it is not necessary to name it so, it's a good convention though
cat my_script.sh                        # touch file1.txt
```

Now let's run this script by giving it to "bash" (Bourne Again SHell) which just runs each line:

```bash
bash my_script.sh 
ls -alhS
```

Let's learn some of basic bash syntax: variables (name="Ada"), if/for/while, &&, $(...), functions and comments (#). You can also use these at the linux prompt. We will upgrade `my_script.sh` into a short tour of the main bash features.

```bash
cat > my_script.sh << 'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# this is a comment
# but that first line is not a comment. It is called the "shebang" (scroll below)
name="HUJI"                           # a variable: no spaces around =
echo "Hello, $name"                   # $name is replaced inside " "
echo 'Hello, $name'                   # but not inside ' '
echo "Today is $(date +%F)"           # $(...) pastes in a command's output "date +%F" prints out YYYY-MM-DD format
echo "This script is called $0"       # $0 is the script's own name, it's preset special variable
echo "I got $# arguments; the first is $1"   # $# counts them, $1 is first, another preset special variable, $2 is second, etc
if true; then                         # the simplest if: true always succeeds
  echo "trivial if statement"
fi                                    # close out the if-else with "fi"
if [ -f file1.txt ]; then             # test: does the file exist? (see [...] explanation below)
  echo "file1.txt exists"
else
  echo "file1.txt is missing"
fi
for i in 1 2 3; do                    # repeat for each item in a list
  echo "round $i"
done
greet() {                             # declare a function: a named block of commands, arguments are optional
  echo "Hi, $1!"                      # if there's a first argument
}
greet
greet Bob                             
greet Bob Alex
EOF
```

That creates the multiline file from the prompt. Now we run it

```bash
bash my_script.sh                     # run it
bash my_script.sh 52002 52019         # run it with two arguments: $1 $2 ...
```

**What is `[ -f file1.txt ]`?** It is not the special `if` condition syntax. It is the same as the `test` command in linux. 
This command returns to an "exit status" like a program, not to the screen (more on this later). It is an ordinary command, made of four separate words:

| Piece | What it is |
|-------|------------|
| `[` | The name of a command (the same one as `test`). It is a real program, and also built into bash. |
| `-f` | An option meaning "is it a regular file that exists?" |
| `file1.txt` | The argument: the file to check. |
| `]` | The last argument. It does nothing except close the pair of brackets. |

Because `[` is a command, every piece needs spaces around it. The command prints nothing; it only sets its exit status (0 if the test is true, 1 if not), and `if` simply runs whatever command follows it and checks that status. This is also why `if true` works: `true` is also a command that always exits 0.

```bash
[ -f file1.txt ]              # nothing is printed! But that doesn't mean it didn't work
echo $?                       # $? stores the exit status (in our case, 0 if the file exists, 1 if not)
[ -f file1.txt ]; echo $?     # two linux commands on one line, separated by a semicolon
[ ! -f file1.txt ]; echo $?   # negation of [ -f file1.txt ]
test -f file1.txt; echo $?    # identical: test is [ without the ]
[-f file1.txt]                # error: command not found (no space after [)
[ -f file1.txt]               # error: missing ']' (no space before ])
[ -d results ]; echo $?       # is it a directory?
[ -s covid.csv ]; echo $?     # exists and is not empty?
[ "$a" = "$b" ]; echo $?      # are the strings equal? (spaces around = required). Fails because it doesn't have context for $a, $b
[ $n -gt 5 ]; echo $?         # is n greater than 5? Fails because it doesn't have context for $n
```

**The shebang.** The first line, `#!/usr/bin/env bash`, is called the **shebang** (from "sharp" `#` and "bang" `!`). It tells the system which program should run the file when you execute it directly, as we will see below. For a Python script it would be `#!/usr/bin/env python3`, and for an R script `#!/usr/bin/env Rscript`. A few details:

- It must be the very first line of the file: no blank line or space before it.
- `env bash` means "find `bash` wherever it is installed on this computer". Executable programs need absolute paths. That is more portable than writing a fixed path like `#!/bin/bash`, because the location differs between systems (for example on a Mac with a newer bash from Homebrew).
- When you run `bash my_script.sh`, you already chose the program yourself, so bash treats the line as an ordinary comment, because it starts with `#`.

Now run the script as an "executable program" instead of handing it to bash. This has a few advantages
* you don't need to know what program executes the code inside (the shebang handles it)
* you can set this program in PATH and access it globally
* other programs can call this program easily

Let's try it:

```bash
./my_script.sh                        # error: Permission denied (see below)
```

The last line fails because the file is not marked as something the computer may run. That is what permissions control, and we fix it next. (We write a more useful script later in this lecture.)

**Permissions.** In the output of `ls -l`, the first column has a string which is always 10 characters: one for the type of item, then three groups of three. Then there are two strings which tell you who is the owner and which group has rights

```bash
ls -alh
```

What do these characters mean? The following is the default permissions:

```
 - rw- r-- r--
 | |   |   |
 | |   |   +-- 8-10: permissions for everyone else ("other")
 | |   +------ 5-7:  permissions for the group (we won't go into this)
 | +---------- 2-4:  permissions for the owner (the user who owns the file)
 +------------ 1:    the type of item (`-` for ordinary file, `d` for directory, `l` for links which we may use later)
```

Am I "kapelner"?

```bash
whoami
```

When using the prompt you are a user and that user has certain permissions for each file and directory. For "real" servers, there are tons of users on the same system, so security becomes more important.

The three letters of each group always come in the order `r`, `w`, `x` and `-` means not granted.

|   | on a file | on a directory |
|---|-----------|----------------|
| `r` | read the contents (`cat`, `head`) | list the names inside (`ls`) |
| `w` | change the contents | create, delete and rename files inside |
| `x` | run it as a program | enter it (`cd`) and reach the files inside |

Some strings you will meet:

| String | What it means |
|--------|---------------|
| `-rw-r--r--` | an ordinary data file: the owner can read and write, everyone else can only read |
| `-rwxr-xr-x` | a ordinary program file: everyone can run it, only the owner can change it |
| `drwxr-xr-x` | an ordinary directory: everyone can enter and list its files, only the owner can change it |
| `-rw-------` | a private file: only the owner can touch it (for passwords and keys) |

The file `my_script.sh` we just created is `-rw-r--r--`. Nobody has an `x`, which is exactly why `./my_script.sh` said `Permission denied`. We need to "change its mode" via `chmod`

```bash
ls -lha
chmod +x my_script.sh   # make it executable for everyone:
ls -lha
./my_script.sh          # now it executes
```

If this is my private script, then maybe I want to make sure nobody else has access to it:

```bash
chmod 600 my_script.sh  # the "600" controls the locations of the permissions - read about it if you care
                        # I've memorized a few of these numeric codes
ls -lha                 #now only i can read and write
chmod u+x my_script.sh  #and only i can execute
ls -lha
./my_script.sh          # now executes (the `./` is execute this one right here to avoid name clashes if they exist)
```

If this can be used and edited by everyone (not usually recommended), then

```bash
chmod 777 my_script.sh
ls -lha
```

Let's talk about the root user (or "super" user, the administrator of the machine). You will definitely 
need to know about this. For example:

```bash
ls -l /etc/security/limits.conf
```

This file controls resource limits and may need to be changed for certain big data
operations. It makes sense only the server admin should be able to change this. Look at the owner and the 
permissions. What does this grant me?


Let's try adding my setting to it

```bash
echo "my special new line" >> /etc/security/limits.conf
```

Fail. I don't have rights. Can I give myself access?

```bash
chmod a+w /etc/security/limits.conf
```

Fail. I'm not the owner. We will return to this later.

###move this up to script

## Your own commands: `PATH`, `export` and `alias`

The `PATH` is a list of directories. When you type a command name, the shell looks for it in each of them 

```bash
echo $PATH
cu #tab-tab
```

A good place for your own scripts is a `bin` folder in your home directory:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/bin                     # a folder for your own programs
cp my_script.sh ~/bin/             # put the script there
export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"      # add ~/bin to the front of the PATH
cd ~                               # navigate elsewhere (where my_script.sh is not found)
ls -alh
which my_script.sh                 # now the shell finds it...
my_script.sh                       #we don't need './' because it's not in the home directory
```

The `export PATH` change lasts only as long as this terminal window. How to fix? To make it permanent, add the line to the file that the shell reads whenever it starts, `~/.bashrc` on Ubuntu (`~/.zshrc` on a Mac). An **alias** is a shortcut for a longer command, and it belongs in the same file:

```bash
echo 'export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.bashrc    # for every new terminal
```

You can also make cute shortcuts for yourself:

```bash
echo "alias ll='ls -lha'" >> ~/.bashrc               # a shortcut: ll
source ~/.bashrc                    # read the file now, instead of reopening
type ll                             # what kind of name is ll?
ll
```


# Editing in the terminal

On a remote server there is no graphical editor, so you need to be able to edit a file in the terminal. The two common terminal editors are `vi` and `nano`. We will only use `vi`; you can learn `nano` on your own.

::: {.callout-note}
## Which is used more, vi or nano?
Vi, by about two to one. In the 2025 Stack Overflow Developer Survey, 24.3% of developers said they use Vim and 12.2% use Nano. Another 14% use Neovim, a modern rewrite of Vim, so the vi family together is ahead by more than three to one. Also, you can count on finding vi. It's installed on virtually every Unix system, including bare servers and containers where nothing else is installed.
:::

However, it has a learning curve. It has **modes**, which is what confuses everyone at first.

```bash
vi covid.csv
```

The survival kit:

| Keys | What it does |
|------|--------------|
| `:<cmd>` +Enter | Run a `vi` command |
| `:set nu` +Enter | Add line numbers |
| `i` | Enter insert mode: now you can type |
| Esc | Leave insert mode |
| `:767` +Enter | Go to line number 767 |
| `gg` | Go to the top of the file (in insert mode) |
| `G` | Go to the bottom of the file (in insert mode) |
| Ctrl+F | Go forward = down one page (in insert mode) |
| Ctrl+B | Go back = up one page (in insert mode) |
| `:w` +Enter | Save |
| `:q` +Enter | Quit |
| `:wq` +Enter | Save and quit |
| `:q!` +Enter | Quit **without** saving |
| `/word` +Enter | Search for "word" (`n` for next match) |
| `d3` | Delete 3 lines (`dd` a/lone deletes one) |
| `u` | Undo |


If you're ever stuck in `vi`, press Esc a few times, then type `:q!` and Enter.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Practice later
`vimtutor` is a 30-minute interactive vi tutorial. On Ubuntu, install it with `sudo apt install vim`.
:::

Back to permissions. What if I need to edit a file that only the administrator can edit?

```bash
vi /etc/security/limits.conf
```

You need to use "sudo" (i.e. super user do)

```bash
sudo vi /etc/security/limits.conf
```

Now of course, you need to actually *be* a super user to do this. That is, another super user gave it to you, 
or you set up the machine yourself. If its your MAC or you set up WSL, you are super user.
Later in the semester, when we login to the university's machines, maybe not, unless they're
giving you a carved out virtual environment. We will see later as I don't know how they set up their machines.

You've seen `sudo` during your setup. You used it to update and install programs e.g. this will
go to ubuntu's servers (and whatever other servers that catalog programs) and see if you have
any updates available for what you have installed. The next line will do upgrades on anything
that needs updating.

```bash
sudo apt update
sudo apt upgrade #if necessary
```

# Looking at data without opening it

A file can be far larger than what you want to (or can) load into memory, but you can still look at it.

We will now return to our downloaded file. The columns are `date`, `county`, `state`, `fips` 
(a numeric code for the county), `cases` and `deaths`. Source: The New York Times, based 
on reports from state and local health agencies, <https://github.com/nytimes/covid-19-data>.

```bash
cat covid.csv         # print the whole file (bad idea for big files!)
less covid.csv        # scroll through a file (q quits, / searches)
head covid.csv        # first 10 lines
head -n 3 covid.csv   # first 3 lines
tail covid.csv        # last 10 lines
tail -n 3 covid.csv   # last 3 lines
```

# Pipes (similar to redirection)

A redirect connects a command usually to a **file**. A **pipe** connects a command to **another command**. 
The symbol is `|`, called the pipe or the vertical bar. It sends the stdout of the command on its left 
into the stdin of the command on its right:

```
command1 | command2        # command1's output becomes command2's input
```

Compare the two ways of counting the first three lines of a file. With a redirect, you need to 

```bash
head -n 3 covid.csv > first3.txt   # with a redirect: save to a file...
wc -l < first3.txt                 # ...then feed the file to the next command
rm first3.txt                      # clean up after yourself!
```

Much easier with a pipe command:

```bash
head -n 3 covid.csv | wc -l        # with a pipe: both steps at once, no file
#^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^   ^^^^^
#     producer        consumer
```
 A few more small ones:

```bash
ls | wc -l                    # how many items are in this folder?
ls -l | head -n 3             # only the first 3 lines of a long listing
echo "hello world" | wc -w    # 2: the text from echo became wc's input
```

You can chain as many commands as you like. Each one does one small job:

```bash
tail covid.csv | sort | uniq  #we'll see the sort and uniq commands soon
```
Pipes process data as a **stream**: each command reads a line, handles it, and passes it on. None of these commands loads the whole file into memory, which is why they work on files much bigger than your RAM. This is the idea behind the one-pass algorithms (which we may see later). For example:

```bash
cat covid.csv | head
```

`cat` does not load the file. It reads a block (around 128 KB), sends it to the pipe, and repeats. Its memory use is tiny, however large the file is. Above when we ran `cat covid.csv`, it started printing immediately. If it had to load the whole file first, nothing would appear until the load finished.

A pipe has a small buffer, and that is what keeps it streaming. On Linux the pipe holds about 64 KB. When it is full, the producer (the command on the left) is paused until the consumer (the command on the right) catches up. This is called backpressure. So even a 100 GB file can usually pass through `cat | ... | ...` using a few megabytes in total, with all the commands running at the same time.

Once `head` quits, cat gets a "broken pipe" signal and stops, so it never bothers to read from the rest of the file.

Here's a nice example of pipe usage. To read a CSV comfortably, line up the columns with the `column` command:

```bash
head covid.csv | column -s, -t    # -s, : fields are separated by commas, -t : table format
```

## Searching with grep

`grep` (global regular expression print) prints the lines of its input argument that match a pattern. We will demo this 
using our dataset as the input argument and use "| head" to limit the results shown to screen or "| wc -l" to count.

```bash
grep "Alaska" covid.csv | head -n 4     # lines containing Alaska
grep -i "alaska" covid.csv | head -n 4  # -i: ignore upper/lower case
grep -v "Alaska" covid.csv | head -n 4  # -v: lines that do NOT match
grep -c "Alaska" covid.csv              # -c: count matching lines
grep -vc "Alaska" covid.csv             # options combine: count the others
grep -n "Alaska" covid.csv | head -n 4  # -n: show line numbers
grep -m 2 "Alaska" covid.csv            # -m 2: stop after 2 matches (the color highlighting is my terminal being smart)
grep -o "2020-03-[0-9][0-9]" covid.csv | head -n 2   # -o: print out only the match component
grep -c "Ada" covid.csv                 # compare: also counts Adams, Adair
grep -m 1 -C 2 "Anchorage" covid.csv    # -C 2: 2 lines of context
```

You can search for several things at once, and in many files:

```bash
grep -e "Alaska" -e "Hawaii" covid.csv | wc -l    # -e: either pattern
grep -f pats.txt covid.csv | wc -l      # -f: patterns listed in a file
grep -F "." covid.csv | wc -l           # -F: literal text, not a pattern
grep -l "Alaska" sample.csv covid.csv   # -l: only NAMES of files that match
grep -c "Alaska" sample.csv covid.csv   # a count for each file
grep -r "Cook" . | head -n 3            # -r: search every file under here
grep -rl "Cook" .                       # ...and just list which files
grep -r --include="*.csv" -l "Cook" .   # ...but only in csv files
```

`grep` also reports whether it found anything, through its **exit status**, which every command has: 0 means success, anything else means failure. The special variable `$?` holds the status of the last command:

```bash
grep "Alaska" covid.csv > /dev/null; echo $?    # 0: found
grep "Atlantis" covid.csv; echo $?              # 1: not found
grep -q "Alaska" covid.csv; echo $?             # -q: quiet, only the status
```

The exit status is what scripts use to make decisions.

**`grep` after another command.** So far `grep` read a file. It can also read the output of any other command through a pipe, which makes it a filter: the first command produces a lot of output, and `grep` keeps only the lines you care about. When no file name is given, `grep` reads its input from the pipe.

```bash
ls | grep csv                       # only the names containing csv
ls -l | grep "^d"                   # only directories: their line starts with d
ls -l | grep -v "^d"                # -v: everything except directories
find . -name "*.csv" | grep covid   # csv files whose path also contains covid
find . -type f | grep -v "\.git/"   # all files, but skip anything inside .git
df -h | grep -v tmpfs               # disk usage without the tmpfs lines
env | grep "^HOME"                  # one environment variable
history | grep chmod                # find that command you ran last week
```

Notice that the first command does the broad work and `grep` narrows it down. You can keep going, e.g. `find . -type f | grep csv | grep -v old | wc -l` counts the csv files that are not "old".

## Regular expressions (for you at home)

A **regular expression** (regex) is a pattern that describes a set of strings. We have been using the simplest regex, a plain word that matches itself. The real power comes from special characters. A few meet you almost everywhere (R, Python, SQL, text editors), so learning them pays off all semester.

| Pattern | Matches | Example |
|---------|---------|---------|
| `.` | any one character | `Co.k` matches Cook |
| `*` | the previous thing, zero or more times | `Co*k` matches Ck, Cok, Coook |
| `+` | the previous thing, one or more times | `Co+k` matches Cok but not Ck |
| `?` | the previous thing, zero or one times | `Lou?isiana` matches Loisiana and Louisiana |
| `^` | the start of the line | `^2020-03` |
| `$` | the end of the line | `,0$` |
| `[abc]` | one character from the set | `[BC]ook` |
| `[a-z]`, `[0-9]` | one character from a range | `[0-9][0-9]` |
| `[^,]` | one character NOT in the set | `[^,]*` is "a field" |
| `{n}`, `{n,m}` | repeat exactly n, or n to m, times | `[0-9]{5}` |
| <code>a&#124;b</code> | either a or b | <code>Texas&#124;Ohio</code> |
| `( )` | group things together | <code>(Texas&#124;Ohio),</code> |
| `\.` | a literal special character | `\.` is a real dot |

Use `grep -E` ("extended") whenever your pattern has `+ ? | ( ) { }`, otherwise `grep` wants a backslash before each of them. Also put patterns in **single quotes**, so the shell doesn't try to interpret characters like `*`, `$` or `|` before `grep` sees them.

Anchors first, `^` and `$`:

```bash
grep '^2020-03-15' covid.csv | head -n 2       # lines that START with a date
grep -c ',0$' covid.csv                        # lines that END with ,0
grep -c '^2020-0[1-3]' covid.csv               # January to March: a set
grep -Ec '^2020-(03|04)-' covid.csv            # March or April: alternatives
grep -E '^2020-03-1[0-5],' covid.csv | wc -l   # March 10 to 15
grep -x 'date,county,state,fips,cases,deaths' covid.csv   # -x: whole line
```

Repetition and wildcards inside a pattern:

```bash
grep -c 'New .*City' covid.csv          # .* is "anything": New ... City
grep -E 'o+k' covid.csv | head -n 1     # one or more o, then k: Cook
grep -E 'Lou?isiana' covid.csv | head -n 1    # the u is optional
grep -E 'a{2}' covid.csv | head -n 1    # a double "aa"
grep -E ',[0-9]{6,},[0-9]+$' covid.csv | head -n 2    # 100,000 cases or more
```

Precision: the `[^,]*` idiom means "any run of characters that isn't a comma", i.e. one CSV field. It lets you say which column you mean:

```bash
# columns: date , county , state , ...  so the state is after two commas
grep -Ec '^[^,]*,[^,]*,Texas,' covid.csv    # only rows whose STATE is Texas
grep ',Texas,' covid.csv | grep -v '^[^,]*,[^,]*,Texas,'
```

The last line shows the 495 impostors. Missing values are easy to find as well. The `fips` column is empty for New York City (the data combines its five boroughs) and for the rows marked "Unknown", so those rows contain two commas in a row:

```bash
grep -c ',,' covid.csv                       # rows with an empty field
grep ',,' covid.csv | head -n 2              # which ones?
grep -E '^[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2},' covid.csv | wc -l    # valid dates
grep -Ev '^[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2},' covid.csv           # the odd ones out
grep -E '^2020-03-15,(New York City|Baldwin),' covid.csv    # a group
```

The last two lines of that block show why `grep` is a data-cleaning tool: the fourth finds rows that do *not* look like data (here, the header), which is how you spot problems in a file too big to read. The same idea works with files that have comment lines:

```bash
printf '# settings\nname=x\n\n# more\nn=3\n' > cfg.txt
grep -v '^#' cfg.txt                  # drop the comment lines
grep -c '^$' cfg.txt                  # ^$ is an empty line: count them
grep -v -e '^#' -e '^$' cfg.txt       # drop comments AND blank lines
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Wildcards vs. regular expressions
Both are patterns, and the characters look alike, but they are different languages. In the shell, `*.csv` means "any name ending in .csv". The same thing as a regex is `.*\.csv$`: `.` is any character, `*` repeats it, `\.` is a real dot, and `$` is the end. In particular, the wildcard `*` stands alone, while the regex `*` repeats the thing before it. The shell uses wildcards for file *names*, and `grep` uses regular expressions for text *inside* files.
:::


## Finding and stopping a process

`tail -f` keeps showing new lines as they are added to a file, which is how you watch a log of a long-running job. To try it, open a second terminal and run the first line, which adds the date to `logfile.txt` every second. Then, in the first terminal, run the second line. Press Ctrl+C in both when done.

```bash
cd ~/workspace/HUJI_52002_Fall_2026/scratch/lec01    # terminal 2
while true; do date >> logfile.txt; sleep 1; done    # terminal 2
tail -f logfile.txt                                  # terminal 1 .... then CTRL+C...
```

What if we forget to close terminal 2?

Every running program is a **process** with an ID number (its **PID**). Let's open a third terminal. The command `ps` lists processes:

```bash
ps                    # your processes in this terminal (not super interesting)
                      # note "bash" is running - it's the program actually receiving your prompt commands
ps -u $USER           # just your processes, from every terminal
ps aux                # every process on the machine
```

In `ps aux`, `a` means processes of all users, `u` means a user-oriented format (with the owner, PID, `%CPU`, `%MEM` and command) and `x` includes programs that have no terminal. To find one process by name, filter the list with a pipe + `grep`:

```bash
ps aux | grep sleep   # find a process by name (grep filters the list)
```

I'll see something like this:

```
USER      PID     %CPU %MEM  VSZ   RSS   TTY    STAT START TIME COMMAND
kapelner  2200782  0.0  0.0  17644 7936  pts/0  S+   23:45 0:00 sleep 300
```

For the columns not self explanatory:
- `PID` indicates the linux process id number
- `VSZ` is the memory reserved
- `RSS` is memory occupied
- `TTY` is the terminal ID the process is connected to
- `STAT` is status (where S+ means sleeping)

**Why did we search for `sleep` and not for `while`?** There is no program called `while`. The loop is part of the bash language, so it is run by the shell itself, the `bash` in terminal 2. What you can see is the command in the loop's children: every second it executes `sleep 1`.

To watch processes live instead, use `htop`, and press `q` to quit:

```bash
htop
```

F4 filters the list (type `sleep`), F9 sends a signal to the selected process, and `q` quits.

**Stopping a process.** The command `kill` takes a PID. Despite its name, it sends the process a **signal**, and the default signal is a polite request to stop, which lets the program clean up (close files, remove temporary data):

```bash
kill 4702             # ask process 4702 to stop (signal SIGTERM)
kill -9 4702          # force it to stop at once (SIGKILL): last resort
```

`kill -9` cannot be refused, but the program gets no chance to clean up and may leave half-written files behind, so try plain `kill` first. You can only stop your own processes. Someone else's, or root's, needs `sudo`. Let's try it:

```bash
ps aux | grep sleep   # find a process by name (grep filters the list)
kill <num> 
```

That didn't work because the PID changes every second! We need to find the PID of the parent of this process
(i.e., the bash program running it)

```bash
ps -axo pid,ppid,command | grep "sleep"   # PID, parent PID, command
ps 418990
```

Now let's stop it gracefully

```bash
kill 418990
ps aux | grep sleep
```

Didn't work. Let's force it to stop:

```bash
kill -9 418990
ps aux | grep sleep
```

Our loop teaches two lessons about this:

- Stop the parent, not the child.
- Interactive shells ignore the polite request. `kill 4702` on the shell in terminal 2 appears to do nothing, because an interactive shell ignores SIGTERM. `kill -9 4702` works, but it ends the shell itself, and terminal 2 usually closes. The normal way to stop a loop is **Ctrl+C in its own terminal**, which sends the process a different signal, SIGINT (number 2).

## Columns, sorting and counting

`cut` picks columns, `sort` orders lines, and `uniq` collapses repeated lines. They are the backbone of command-line data analysis:

```bash
#date,county,state,fips,cases,deaths
cut -d, -f1,3 covid.csv | head -n 10     # columns 1 and 3
cut -d, -f1,3  covid.csv | head -n 10 | sort -r     # columns 1 and 3 most recent first
cut -d, -f1,3  covid.csv | sort -r | head -n 10     # why is this slower?
cut -d, -f1,3 covid.csv | head -n 10     # columns 1 and 3 most recent first
cut -d, -f2-4 covid.csv | head -n 4     # columns 2 through 4
cut -d, -f2-4 covid.csv | head -n 4 | uniq    #same output just pruned to unique rows
cut -d, -f2-4 covid.csv | head -n 4 | uniq -c #counts the unique rows
cut -d, -f4- covid.csv | head -n 4      # column 4 to the end
cut -c1-7 covid.csv | head -n 4         # characters 1-7: not columns at all (the seven charas YYYY-MM in this case)
cut -c1-7 covid.csv | uniq -c   # number of cases per month, most recent first
cut -c1-7 covid.csv | uniq -c | sort -nr   # sorted as a number (not text), largest first
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## `cut` doesn't understand quoted fields
`cut -d, -f2` splits at *every* comma, even one inside quotes. For a file with a line `"Smith, John",Boston`, column 2 comes out as ` John"` instead of `Boston`. `covid.csv` has no quoted fields, so we are safe here, but real CSV files often do. Check with `grep -c '"'` first, and use a tool that understands CSV (R, Python, DuckDB) when it matters:

```bash
printf 'name,city\n"Smith, John",Boston\n' > quoted.csv
cut -d, -f2 quoted.csv
```
:::


To sort a CSV by a column, tell `sort` the separator with `-t` and the column with `-k`. Write the column twice, `-k5,5`, so it sorts on that column alone and not everything after it:

```bash
#date,county,state,fips,cases,deaths
sort -t, -k5,5 -n -r covid.csv | head -n 30   # largest case counts, any county
sort -t, -k3,3 -k5,5nr covid.csv | head -n 30 # state, then cases (high to low)
sort -t, -k4,4 -u covid.csv | wc -l          # one row per distinct fips code
```

`uniq` removes repeated lines, but only repeated *neighbors*, which is why it almost always follows a `sort`:

```bash
printf 'a\nb\na\na\nc\n' | uniq               # a b a c: neighbors only
printf 'a\nb\na\na\nc\n' | sort | uniq        # a b c
printf 'a\nb\na\na\nc\n' | sort | uniq -c     # with counts: 3 a, 1 b, 1 c
```

Put them together and you can answer real questions about a file with 885,000 rows in a few seconds:

```bash
#date,county,state,fips,cases,deaths
cut -d, -f3 covid.csv | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 5   # top 5 states
cut -d, -f3 covid.csv | sort -u | wc -l           # how many distinct "states"?
cut -d, -f2,3 covid.csv | sort -u | wc -l         # distinct county-state pairs
grep -E ',(Texas|Ohio),' covid.csv | cut -d, -f1,2,5 | head -n 2
```

The pattern `sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head` is a useful idiom: *count how often each value occurs, and show the most common first*.


## Chaining commands and exit status

Recall that every command ends with an exit status: 0 for success, anything else for failure. The shell can chain commands based on it:

```bash
echo a; echo b                    # ; runs both, whatever happens
mkdir results && cd results       # && : second only if the first worked
pwd
cd ..
cd /nonexistent && echo "arrived in /nonexistent" # the echo never runs
cd /nonexistent || echo "never arrived in /nonexistent"  # || : second only if first failed
grep -q "Alaska" covid.csv && echo "found it"
grep -q "Atlantis" covid.csv || echo "not there"
```
